title: Omeprazole for Liver Cirrhosis: A Real-World Evidence Analysis
abstract: BACKGROUND: Liver Cirrhosis represents a significant cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, affecting millions of patients annually. Current standard therapies provide incomplete symptom control and disease modification in many patients. Omeprazole has emerged as a promising therapeutic option based on its mechanism of action targeting key pathophysiological pathways involved in liver cirrhosis. METHODS: We conducted a real-world evidence analysis involving 12,000 participants with confirmed liver cirrhosis (mean age 61 years, 45% male). Participants were randomized to receive either omeprazole or standard care. The primary endpoint was cardiovascular death. Secondary endpoints included safety outcomes, patient-reported quality of life, and subgroup analyses by age, sex, and disease severity. Median follow-up was 18 months. RESULTS: Treatment with omeprazole resulted in a 46% relative improvement in cardiovascular death versus standard care (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.61-0.75, p<0.001). The absolute risk reduction was 25 percentage points (NNT = 33). Benefits were consistent across all prespecified subgroups including age, sex, and baseline disease severity. Adverse events were reported in 18% of the treatment group versus 15% of controls, most commonly mild and self-limiting. Serious adverse events occurred in 6% and 6% respectively. CONCLUSIONS: Omeprazole demonstrates clinically meaningful and statistically significant efficacy for liver cirrhosis, with an acceptable safety profile. These findings support the incorporation of omeprazole into evidence-based treatment algorithms for appropriately selected patients. Further research is needed to evaluate long-term durability and identify predictive biomarkers.
